commands.short: Add an adapter, or change one, by kind
commands.long:
Adds an adapter of a kind from `pando adapter kinds`. Ordinary settings go in --set KEY=VALUE;
a secret setting such as an API key is asked for without echoing it, so it never lands in
your shell history (piped in when stdin is not a terminal). Adding with an existing --id
changes that adapter. Pando loads adapters at startup: restart it afterwards, except after
a source connection or an image registry, which are used from the moment they are saved.

With a kind named, --help lists its settings and their defaults, the advanced ones under
their own heading. Advanced settings take --set like any other.

  pando adapter add ai/anthropic --set model=claude-sonnet-5

flags.name: default
flags.usage: make it the default adapter of its category, in place of the current one (default: only when the category has none)

flags.name: disabled
flags.usage: save it turned off: Pando keeps its settings and does not use it. A secret left empty keeps the stored one

flags.name: id
flags.usage: the adapter's ID (default: the kind's usual prefix and name, e.g. ai_anthropic)

flags.name: name
flags.usage: what the console calls it (default: the kind's name)

flags.name: preset
flags.usage: a known provider's settings to start from, by ID, as `pando adapter kinds` lists them; at a terminal, asked when not given

flags.name: set
flags.usage: a setting, KEY=VALUE; repeat for more

commands.short: Administer this installation from the host
commands.long:
Commands that work against the database directly, for when nobody can sign in.

Running these needs shell access on the host and the configuration that names the
database. That is the whole of the authorization, and it is the same access that
could change the row by hand.

commands.short: Turn password sign-in back on when no identity provider works
commands.long:
Clears disable_password_sign_in in host policy, so local accounts can sign in with a password again.

For when password sign-in is off and nobody can sign in through an identity provider. Follow it with
`pando admin reset-password` if you also need a password for an account.

commands.short: Set a local account's password when nobody can sign in
commands.long:
Sets a new password for a local account, ends every session it has, revokes its API
tokens, and lifts any limit its wrong passwords put on signing in.

The account must change the password again at its next sign-in: this hands a way
back in to somebody, which is not the same as choosing their credential.

Accounts that sign in through an external identity provider are changed where they
live, not here.

flags.name: password
flags.usage: the new password; prompts on a terminal, and generates one otherwise

commands.short: Remove a local account's two-factor authentication when nobody can sign in
commands.long:
Removes a local account's authenticator and recovery codes, ends every session it has,
revokes its API tokens, and lifts any limit its wrong codes put on signing in. It then signs in with its password
alone, and sets two-factor authentication up again there if host policy requires it.

Accounts that sign in through an external identity provider get their second factor
from the provider, not here.

commands.short: Make a new setup token for an installation that is not set up yet
commands.long:
Prints a new one-time setup token and retires the one Pando printed to its log at startup.

A new installation is set up in the console, and the setup form asks for this token, so that
reaching the console first is not enough to become its administrator. Refused once the
installation has an account.

A function with no adapter is off. The draft commands propose and never apply: create
what they draft with pando group and pando policy, or in the console.

commands.short: Show or change where an app is reached
commands.long:
With no flags, shows the app's routing and address, where it moves at the next deploy
if a change is saved, and the routing adapters it could use with the domains each serves.

With flags, changes it. A flag left out keeps what the app has, or takes the adapter's
default when moving to another adapter. --domain puts the app in another of the
adapter's domains, such as a second Cloudflare zone: alone it makes <app>.<domain>, and
with --hostname docs it makes docs.<domain>.

A change is saved as a spec revision and takes effect at the next deploy, when the old
address stops working. Without --confirm nothing is changed and Pando says what would move.
commands.example:
pando app address notes
  pando app address notes --domain trypando.ai --confirm
  pando app address notes --hostname docs.example.com --confirm

flags.name: adapter
flags.usage: the routing adapter, such as rte_cloudflare

flags.name: confirm
flags.usage: make the change; without it Pando only says what would move

flags.name: domain
flags.usage: with subdomain mode: which of the adapter's domains, such as trypando.ai

flags.name: hostname
flags.usage: with subdomain mode: the hostname, or with --domain a single name such as docs

flags.name: mode
flags.usage: subdomain, path or port

flags.name: path
flags.usage: with path mode: the path, such as /team/notes

commands.long:
With --trigger branch (the default), each new commit on the branch deploys. Without
--branch, that is the branch the app was deployed from.

With --trigger release, each new release tag deploys. A release is a tag such as
v1.2.3, or one matching --tag-pattern, a pattern such as release-* where * matches
any characters.

instead of Pando finding out at its next check. It needs Pando to be reachable from
the git host. Paste the URL and secret into the repository's webhook settings, with
content type application/json. The secret is printed this once; making a new one
replaces it.

commands.long:
Deletes an app. Its storage is backed up first and the backup is kept until you
discard it — not aged out.

If the backup fails the app is not deleted, because a failed backup means the data
is not safe. Pass --discard-data to delete without one.

commands.short: Show how far detection has got, and what to do next
commands.long:
Shows where an app's detection stands: running and at which stage, or how it
finished — ready, waiting on answers, blocked or failed — and what to do next.
Questions are printed exactly as Pando wrote them, to paste into whatever wrote
the app.

With --wait, waits for detection to finish, printing each stage as it is
reached. It then exits 0 when the app is ready to accept, 2 when there are
questions to answer, and 1 when detection failed or was blocked.

commands.short: Accept detection's proposal as the app's configuration
commands.long:
Accepts what detection worked out and pins it as the app's configuration. This
does not deploy: `pando deploy <app>` does that.

--env and --secret set variables in the same step; a secret is stored by the
install's secrets adapter. --optional names a dependency the app runs without.

Accepting over an app that is already configured replaces how it is built and
what it runs, and needs --confirm. Variables you set, how each dependency is
filled, and storage you added are carried over. `pando app detection diff <app>`
shows what would change.

commands.short: Answer one of detection's questions
commands.long:
Answers a question detection asked. The key is the one printed with the
question by `pando app detection <app>`.

An answer that changes what is built, such as a build argument, has Pando build
and scan the image again, so the plan shows the score of what will run. This
waits for that, printing each stage, then exits as `pando app detection --wait`
does: 0 when the app is ready to accept, 2 when there are questions left, and 1
when detection failed or was blocked.

commands.long:
Saves the archive — gzipped JSON lines, one audit event per line — to --output, or to
audit-<month>.jsonl.gz in the current directory. The SHA-256 is checked against the archive's
manifest as it arrives, and a file that does not match is removed rather than kept.

commands.short: Export a range of the audit log as gzipped JSON lines
commands.long:
Writes the audit events between --since and --until, in commit order, as gzipped JSON lines:
to --output, or to standard output when that is not a terminal. --since and --until take a time
(2026-09-21T09:00:00Z) or a duration back from now (24h); left out, the range is open at that end.

The export covers the live log only. When the range reaches back before it, a note on standard
error says where the live log starts; `pando audit archives` has the months before that.
commands.example:
pando audit export --since 720h > audit.jsonl.gz
  pando audit export --since 2026-09-01T00:00:00Z --until 2026-10-01T00:00:00Z --format ocsf -o september.jsonl.gz

flags.name: action
flags.usage: only actions starting with this, e.g. grant.; repeatable

flags.name: exclude

commands.long:
An audit sink is a destination, such as a SIEM's syslog or HTTPS collector, that Pando pushes
the audit log to as it is written. This lists each one with what it sends where, the events
waiting to go (BACKLOG), when it last delivered, and its last error. Below the table, each sink's

commands.short: Print the audit log in commit order, one JSON event per line
commands.long:
Prints audit events oldest first, one JSON object per line, from --after: a cursor a previous
run printed, or now for only what happens from here on. Without --after it starts at the oldest
event in the live log. Without --follow it stops once it has caught up; with --follow it keeps
waiting for new events until interrupted.

When it stops, for any reason, it prints the last cursor to standard error as
`cursor: c1.…`. Pass that back as --after to carry on where it left off. Delivery is at least
once: an event can be printed again after a resume, and its id is the key to drop it by.
commands.example:
pando audit tail --follow --after now
  pando audit tail --after c1.AAAA --action grant. --exclude grant.view 2>cursor.txt >>events.jsonl

commands.short: Show whether a newer Pando is released, what changed, and how to upgrade
commands.long:
Shows the version the server runs, the latest release on the update channel, and the
changelog of every version in between, with security fixes and breaking changes marked.
Then the command that upgrades the server. The check is host policy: disable_update_check
turns it off and update_channel chooses stable or prerelease (`pando policy set`).
Pando checks at startup and every six hours; --check asks GitHub now.

commands.short: Upgrade the Pando server in place to a newer release
commands.long:
Upgrades the server to the latest release, or to the version given. Pando verifies the
image's signature, takes a full backup (or not, with --skip-backup), and starts a helper
that replaces Pando's container and puts the previous version back if the new one does
not start. Every app is unreachable while Pando restarts. Needs install.upgrade, and
upgrade_in_place on in host policy. `pando upgrade last` shows how the last one went.
